editorial.headline: Wholesale Building Materials and Tools: Open Nationally, Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This wholesale activity is nationally open to 100% foreign ownership, but Bali’s permanent moratorium blocks PMA registration because every scope is Low or Medium-Low risk at the Large scale.
editorial.body:
This activity is wholesale trade in a broad practical range of construction materials and associated equipment. Its defined scope includes wallpaper; plastic pipes and hoses; Formica; corrugated plastic sheet; flat and layered asbestos cement; asbestos-cement drainage pipes; manual hand tools; electric-powered hand tools; water heaters; and boilers. It is an activity of distribution, bringing those goods into the wholesale market rather than defining a construction service or a retail format. The scope is deliberately concrete: it reaches from wall finishes and piping components to tool lines and heating equipment. The grouping holds together surfaces, sheets and pipe-related goods with manual, electrically powered and heating equipment.

Registration is open at Micro, Small, Medium, and Large scales. The record makes no separate national scale-specific foreign-ownership ceiling among those stated scales. Nationally, the activity is TERBUKA—open to foreign investment—with a maximum foreign ownership of 100%. The national position is therefore clear: foreign participation is permitted up to full ownership under the cited Presidential Regulations. This establishes national availability for the wholesale activity precisely as defined by the scope. It should be read alongside the local registration conditions the record expressly identifies for Bali, because they govern whether a PMA registration can proceed there.

In Bali, the answer changes decisively. A foreigner cannot register this activity in Bali today. At the Large scale, OSS assesses every scope within the activity as Low or Medium-Low risk, and Bali consequently blocks it under the moratorium applying across the island. The rule is permanent: the province blocks PMA registration for all Low- and Medium-Low-risk KBLI activities. The governing issue is not a reduced national ceiling: nationally, the ceiling remains 100%. In Bali, the record instead identifies a risk-classification block and the moratorium as the reason PMA registration cannot proceed. That is the local position that matters at filing.

The practical reading is deliberately two-level. National rules leave full foreign ownership available for the wholesale distribution of the materials, tools, water heaters and boilers listed in the scope. Yet a founder considering Bali must treat the provincial PMA outcome as controlling at the point of registration. National openness does not overcome a permanent, island-wide block where this activity’s scopes carry Low or Medium-Low risk classifications. That separation demands precision: the national PMA setting says what ownership is permitted in the country, while the Bali classification says whether registration is allowed on the island. Both statements can be true at once, and this record requires them to be read together.
